To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

forage-based dairying can be sustained in water-limited environments by: (i) increasing the proportion of forage that is consumed by the cows as grazed feed, and (ii) changing the forage species mix and management to include forages that can be grazed in summer.

1) the use of simulation models to explore the impact of water restrictions on dairy farming in a region of southern Australia that is likely to experience significant water shortages due to climate change, has identified forage options that could sustain farm business profitability, 2) these options include the use of summer-dormant perennial pasture plus a double cropping rotation, and 3) the key to success in this system is to maintain a high level of direct grazing of pasture or crop.

forage-based dairy farming in northern Victoria, with autumn calving, is sustainable under a range of water-allocation scenarios, provided that the forage base is changed and the stocking rate is adjusted accordingly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new dairy farm system management strategies that are capable of sustaining dairy farming profitability in the face on ongoing reductions in irrigation water allocations.
the development of a new paradigm for dairy farming in a water-limted future.

the development and application of simulation models of pasture growth, crop growth and dairy farm system management and performance to investigate the potential to sustain dairy business profitability under water restrictions in northern Victoria, a region of southern Australia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the best adaptation strategy for a dairy farm to respond to water restrictions is to grow as much pasture as possible and to graze it.

a combination of forage-based management strategies and changes to strategic dairy management policies can maintain profitability in a future where dairy farms in the region will have access to 50-60% less irrigation water than at present.

the most important factor determining the ability of the dairy farm to sustain profitability under restricted irrigation water allocations was the ability of the farm system to maintain pasture intake at a level sufficient to sustain milk production.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
forage-based dairying can adapt to water-limited futures in northern Victoria if a range of strategic management changes are made to the base system.

a forage-based dairy system with a diverse forage base (pasture, crop silage, and grazed crop) and with a large proportion of grazed forage can sustain dairy farm profitability in the face, and even in the context of, reduced irrigation water availability.
the most important adaptation to water restrictions is a shift to forage-based systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dairy industry in southern Australian has the capacity to adapt to climate change impacts, including lower, and more variable, water allocations.
the dairy industry will need to adapt to a future of lower and more variable water availability.
the dairy industry in southern Victoria can adapt to lower water allocations, but only if farmers are willing to change the way they manage their farms, including the way they calve their cows.
